open-question.question: The answer sweep today runs its own lift call for each question before recording it, using the call's failure as the per-question skip and its printed line as the commit body, and the answer-with-recommendation procedure it then follows runs the same lift again in its own step 2. With the sweep inline and that procedure's contract now open to change, should the sweep drop its separate lift and use the procedure's own lift instead (its failure treated as the per-question skip, its printed line held as the commit body), or keep a separate lift before following the procedure, so each question is lifted twice?
open-question.alternative: The sweep drops its own lift call and follows answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md from its lift step. The sweep treats a failure of that procedure's lift as the per-question skip and keeps the line that lift prints as the commit body. This is the same way the single-question answer-open-question-with-recommendation skill already keeps the procedure's lift print for its commit. Each question is lifted exactly once. The inline sweep and the single-question skill then run the procedure the same way, so the lift that re-checks the question, gates the skip and supplies the body is also the lift that feeds the recorded ANSWER and RECORDED OPTION. The two can never drift apart. The procedure's no-recommendation guard currently says to stop and report the tool's Error: line, but the sweep needs a silent skip that moves on. So either the procedure's guard wording or the sweep's text has to separate a lift failure, which is a skip, from any later failure after the fold, which stops the whole run. That boundary then sits inside a shared file that the single-question skill also follows.

The sweep keeps its own lift call per question as the re-check, skip and commit-body source, and only then follows answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md unchanged. The procedure lifts the same block a second time in its own step. The procedure's contract and its stop-on-failed-lift guard stay exactly as they are. The skip decision is made before the procedure starts, so the procedure's guard can never fire inside the sweep. The sweep's per-question structure also stays what the CLAUDE.md sweep invariant describes today: the lift call itself is the re-check. Every question costs a redundant tool call and a second read of the lifted line. Both lifts must be described in the skill, which duplicates prose. The sweep has to make clear which print it keeps as the body, even though nothing writes between the two calls so they cannot differ.

The sweep keeps its own single lift as re-check, skip and body source. It skips answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md and hands the lifted line as ANSWER, plus the text before the first spaced em dash as RECORDED OPTION, straight to the recording core, answer-procedure.md. One lift per question, and neither shared procedure's contract changes. The sweep controls the skip-versus-stop boundary in its own text, and the recording core already accepts a caller-supplied ANSWER and RECORDED OPTION. The goal says the sweep runs the shared answer-with-recommendation procedure itself, so the goal would need rewording. The derivation of RECORDED OPTION from the lifted line would be written out in two places. And once the sweep leaves, answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md has only one runner, the single-question skill, which conflicts with the project rule that a shared file needs two or more runners and would push the procedure toward being inlined.

answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md gains an optional pre-lifted ANSWER input. The sweep lifts once itself, for the re-check, skip and body, and passes that line in. The procedure runs its own lift only when the line is not supplied, as in the single-question skill. One lift per question. The sweep still formally follows the shared procedure as the goal says, and the skip stays decided in the sweep before the procedure starts. The procedure would branch on whether an input was supplied. The recorded milestone-resolution decision rules that pattern out for MILESTONE_DIR ("neither procedure branches on whether the input was supplied"). It also adds a second path through a shared file for a saving of one cheap tool call per question.
open-question.recommendation: One lift per question is what the goal describes (the procedure's lift as the re-check) and how the single-question skill already keeps the procedure's print as its commit body; the skip-versus-stop boundary is already drawn by the mid-question failure decision, which stops the run only after a fold, so the procedure's guard need only stop without changing anything and leave what follows to the caller. Keep separate lift pays a redundant call to describe the same print twice, Sweep delegates to core leaves the shared procedure one runner and contradicts the goal's wording, and Optional pre-lifted input reintroduces the supplied-or-not branch the milestone-resolution decision ruled out.

open-question.question: The goal still describes an end-of-run check in which a walk call's print is reported as the still-skipped advisory, while the recorded skipped-question decision has the sweep name no skipped question and add no end-of-run call to find them. Does the inline sweep keep any end-of-run walk call at all, and if it does not, is the goal's end-of-run sentence to be revised so the two documents agree?
open-question.alternative: The inline sweep makes no end-of-run walk call. The goal's end-of-run sentence is then revised through `/modify-milestone-goal`, either dropped or reworded to say the sweep ends on its terse status line or no-op line, so the goal and the recorded skipped-question decision describe the same shape. The two documents stop contradicting each other at the source. Later readers, `derive-tasks`, and the task that rewrites the sweep SKILL.md see one consistent end-of-run shape. That shape already matches the recorded decision (no record of failed lifts, no end-of-run call) and the CLAUDE.md invariant that stripped dependents get no console advisory. It takes a separate goal edit through `/modify-milestone-goal`, which only acts and never cascades, so it runs as its own step on top of recording this answer. The goal also loses the "still-skipped questions" phrasing it shares with the CLAUDE.md reporting invariant. That invariant's advisory list then needs its own check to see whether "still-skipped questions" still describes any runner.

The inline sweep makes no end-of-run walk call, and this is recorded under `## Decisions` as overriding the goal's end-of-run sentence, which is left as written. The decision governs wherever the two differ. It is the cheapest resolution. One answer commit settles the behaviour with no goal edit, and the recorded decision already carries the operative rule, so nothing new has to be designed. The Goal section keeps a sentence the milestone has decided against. `derive-tasks`, the completion procedure, and any later review pass read the goal first and may build or flag the end-of-run walk again. The next `/review-milestone-requirements` run is likely to raise this same mismatch as a new open question.

The inline sweep keeps one end-of-run `walk` call, but not as a skipped-question advisory. Any id it prints means a recommendation-bearing block was left unrecorded, and that is reported as an anomaly beside the terse line. The goal sentence is revised to describe this check in place of the still-skipped advisory. It keeps a cheap, live, tool-based check that the run left no recommendation-bearing block behind, with no re-read of the document. It also stays within the recorded decision's letter, since it never finds or names skipped questions. The check is close to a no-op. A `lift` fails only when a block is gone or carries no `<recommendation>`, and `walk` lists only recommendation-bearing blocks. After a single pass that records or stops, that leaves `walk` nothing to print unless something outside the run changed the document. The skill would gain a step and a reporting branch that almost never fires. It also goes against the spirit of the skipped-question decision's "no end-of-run call".
open-question.recommendation: The recorded skipped-question decision already rules out an end-of-run call and any naming of skipped questions, so the goal's still-skipped sentence is a leftover contradiction that derive-tasks and the next review pass would read first; revising it through /modify-milestone-goal removes the mismatch at its source, whereas Decision supersedes leaves the goal describing behaviour the milestone decided against and Walk as completeness check adds a step and a reporting branch that a single pass can never make fire.

open-question.question: The goal says a contradiction the sweep happens to notice is reported once beside the terse status line while the run proceeds, but not what counts as one or what the advisory carries. Does a contradiction cover only a pick against an entry already under Decisions, or also a pick against a decision the same run recorded earlier and a pick against another standing pick, and does the advisory name the Short Titles and decisions involved or stay identifier-free?
open-question.alternative: A contradiction is only a recorded pick that runs against an entry already under `## Decisions` when the run started, as seen in the whole-set snapshot read before the loop. The advisory is one fixed line with no identifiers that says a recorded answer may conflict with an earlier decision and points at the run's commits. This is the smallest reading. The snapshot already holds the pre-run Decisions section, so the sweep only has to remember that it saw a conflict. One fixed line with no identifiers matches the terse reporting convention and the recorded skipped-question and new-question decisions, which keep no per-item record during the loop. It misses the likeliest conflict in an unattended run: a later pick against a decision the same run recorded a moment earlier. The recommendation pass chose those picks against the pre-run document, not against each other's recorded results. The line without identifiers also leaves the user to search a stack of `Recommendation-answer:` commits to find which answer is at fault before a revert-then-re-answer.

A contradiction is a recorded pick that runs against any entry in the live `## Decisions` section at fold time. That covers entries that existed before the run and ones the run added itself, and it is exactly the answer core's analyse-step check ("does it contradict or supersede anything already written in the document?"). The single advisory names each conflicting pair: the answered question's Short Title and the Decisions heading it conflicts with. It reuses the check the answer core already runs on every question against the live `requirements.md`, which the whole-set-read decision says takes precedence over the snapshot. It adds no new analysis and catches conflicts inside the run. Naming the pair tells the user which commit to revert and re-answer, and that is information git does not hold, because a commit diff shows what was folded in, not what it conflicts with. The sweep must keep a list of Short Title and heading pairs across the loop and print a variable-length advisory. That breaks the identifier-free status line style and the "keeps no record during the loop" pattern the skipped-question decision set. It also blurs the line between noticing a conflict and judging a pick, which the goal rules out.

A contradiction is a recorded pick that runs against any entry in the live `## Decisions` section at fold time, whether it was there before the run or recorded earlier in it, which is the answer core's own analyse-step check. The advisory is still one fixed line with no identifiers, printed once beside the status line whenever that check found anything during the run. It covers conflicts inside the run at no new analysis cost. The only state kept across the loop is a single flag, so the reporting keeps the one-fixed-line shape and the no-record-during-the-loop pattern of the sibling reporting decisions. The user learns that something conflicts but not what. To find the pair they have to reread every commit from the run, or `requirements.md`, looking for the conflict the sweep already found and did not report. That undercuts the reason the goal keeps this one advisory when the sweep reports nothing else.

A contradiction covers a recorded pick against any live Decisions entry, before or during the run, and also a pick against another block's standing recommendation that the sweep has not reached yet, found by checking the whole-set snapshot. The advisory names the Short Titles and decisions or picks involved. It catches the widest set of conflicts, including one between two standing picks, before the second pick is recorded. The user sees every conflict the run touched in a single place. A conflict between standing picks is largely already handled. If the recorded decision forces or moots the sibling, the answer core's cascade folds that and removes the sibling. If the sibling's dependency tag assumed another option, `remove --option` strips its pick. What remains is the sweep judging picks it has not recorded yet against the snapshot, which the goal's "never judges picks" rules out. Any such report is also unnecessary once the later pick reaches its own check against the live Decisions section at fold time.
open-question.recommendation: The answer core's analyse step already asks at fold time whether the answer contradicts anything written in the live requirements.md, so noticing a conflict against a decision the same run recorded costs no new analysis and stays noticing rather than judging; the advisory survives the terse rule only because git does not hold which decision a folded answer conflicts with, so it must name the question and the heading or it leaves the user re-reading every commit before a revert-then-re-answer. Prior decisions misses the likeliest in-run conflict, the identifier-free variant carries nothing actionable, and Decisions and standing picks would judge picks the sweep has not reached.

open-question.question: The headless-chain decision lands the page edit only after a confirming run of the new fable-high sweep settings on this repository, but the inline sweep exists only once this milestone's tasks are complete, by which time this milestone's own questions are already answered. Which run counts as the confirming run, and does the documentation task wait within this milestone for a later milestone's first sweep or land on some other confirmation?
open-question.alternative: The page edit is the last task of this milestone and lands inside it. The first inline sweep of the next milestone, run at fable high, counts as the confirming run. If that run falls short, the fix is a revert-then-correct in the milestone that ran it. Milestone 30 already worked this way: its headless-chain task landed within milestone 30 once both skills existed, and the values were checked afterwards against the next milestone's first review pass. This follows the one precedent the run-before-record rule already has. The milestone finishes with its goal fully delivered, documentation and host trees included, and the check still happens on a real sweep over real questions, not on a stand-in. The page names fable high for the sweep before any run has confirmed it. That reverses the plain reading of the recorded decision, which says the edit lands only after a confirming run, so the headless-chain decision's wording would have to be read or revised as landing first and confirming afterwards. Any mismatch is found only after users of the page may have copied the new lines.

Once the inline sweep skill and its host rebuild are complete, the confirming run is made inside this milestone on a scratch branch or worktree. That tree puts back this milestone's own recommended but unrecorded state, for example the tree just before the recent `Recommendation-answer:` commits, carrying the new skill. The sweep then runs there at `--model "fable" --effort high`. The scratch branch is thrown away, and the documentation task, ordered after the skill task, lands once the run matches the committed answers. The run happens before the page records the settings, just as the decision says. It uses real questions from this repository that already have known recorded outcomes to compare against, and nothing waits on a later milestone. It needs a fixture setup the workflow has never used: rebuilding a past document state with a future skill, running a headless sweep against it, and throwing away the commits it makes. It also tests only the few recommendation-bearing questions this milestone had, which may never exercise cascades or contradictions. And the task list gains a manual, non-reproducible step that the completion procedure has to run and verify.

alternative.id: Defer page edit to next milestone

open-question.alternative: This milestone leaves the four answer-sweep lines as they are, at `opus`. That stays runnable, because an inline skill runs on either model. The page edit moves out of scope, and the milestone records that the edit lands in the next milestone once that milestone's first inline sweep has run at fable high. It follows the rule as written. Nothing is recorded before a real run confirms it, the confirming run is a real sweep over new questions, and this milestone needs no fixture work. This milestone's goal lists headless chains among the surfaces it updates, so the goal's scope would have to shrink. The next milestone also inherits a documentation chore that has nothing to do with its own goal, and the page keeps recommending opus for a skill whose cost profile no longer suits it until that milestone gets to it.

No separate run of the sweep is needed. The inline recommendation pass has already run at fable high on this repository, including this milestone's own recommendation annotation. The headless-chain decision says the inline sweep has the same run shape as that line, so that run is taken as the confirmation. The page edit lands with this milestone's other documentation tasks. Nothing waits and no fixture is built. The decision's own argument, that the inline sweep pays for the whole-set context once per run just like the recommend line, is exactly what an earlier run at those settings has already shown works. It confirms a different skill by analogy, not the sweep itself. The sequential folds, cascades, per-answer commits, and the `requirements.md` that keeps growing across one long run are not what a single recommendation pass does, so the run-before-record rule is met in name only. It also sets a precedent that weakens the rule for later settings changes.
open-question.recommendation: Milestone 30's rule as recorded confirms the values against the next milestone's first run of the new skills, and its headless-chain task landed inside milestone 30 exactly that way, so the same reading keeps this milestone's goal whole and confirms on a real sweep over new questions; the recorded decision's after-a-confirming-run wording is read as that precedent. Replay builds a fixture the workflow has never used for a handful of questions, Defer shrinks the goal and hands the next milestone a chore, and the recommend-line run confirms a different skill by analogy.
